title: Finite-Dimensional Type I von Neumann Algebras in PyTorch: A GPU-Accelerated Framework for Random Block-Diagonal Operators
abstract: We present \texttt{torch\_vn\_algebra}, an open-source Python library built on PyTorch for numerical experiments with finite-dimensional Type I von Neumann algebras (direct sums of matrix algebras). The library provides:   $\bullet$ a compact batched tensor representation $(B,C,k_{\max},k_{\max})$ that handles both Monte Carlo samples and multiple direct summands;   $\bullet$ lazy evaluation of operators to avoid unnecessary memory allocation;   $\bullet$ generation of random operators with arbitrary eigenvalue distributions (user-provided samplers) and various unitary ensembles (Haar, $\mathrm{SU}(n)$, COE, CSE, diagonal phases);   $\bullet$ functional calculus via SVD (absolute value, square root, inverse, entropy) and a hybrid method for extreme eigenvalues (exact diagonalisation for $k_{\max}\le256$, otherwise power iteration);   $\bullet$ three trace functionals (blunt, normalised subspace trace, and the von Neumann tracial state);   $\bullet$ GPU-accelerated batched linear algebra for moderate-scale Monte Carlo studies (e.g., $2\times10^4$ samples of $100\times100$ operators).   The library is validated against analytical expectations (Haar moments, trace properties). Performance benchmarks on a Tesla P100 GPU are presented and discussed. Limitations and future work are outlined. The code is open-source.
summary: This paper introduces an open-source PyTorch library designed to perform numerical simulations on finite-dimensional Type I von Neumann algebras. It provides GPU acceleration and advanced tools for calculating observables related to random block-diagonal operators. This allows researchers to study quantum phenomena governed by these algebraic structures in regimes previously inaccessible due to computational cost.
main_problem: Developing efficient numerical tools for Monte Carlo simulations involving finite-dimensional Type I von Neumann algebras.
main_result: The library successfully implements complex calculations on block-diagonal operators, showing significant GPU speedups and confirming expected mathematical inequalities in various quantum observables.
method: It utilizes a custom PyTorch framework with lazy evaluation to handle batched tensor representations of random block-diagonal operators, performing functional calculus via SVD or power iteration.
model_or_system: The model is based on finite-dimensional Type I von Neumann algebras, represented as direct sums of matrix algebras ($ igoplus M_{n_c}(\mathbb{C})$), relevant in quantum mechanics for studying superselection rules and decoherence.
key_observables: Michelson contrast ($\Delta(A)$) and various trace difference quantities ($z$), such as $	ext{Tr}(|XY|) - 	ext{Tr}(|X||Y|)$.
important_parameters: Batch size ($B$), number of direct summands ($C$), and maximum dimension ($k_{\max}$), with performance benchmarks up to $2	imes10^4$ samples.
main_assumptions: The framework is limited to Type I algebras (direct sums) and finite dimensions; SVD becomes a bottleneck for very large dimensions.
figures_summary: Figures show Monte Carlo results validating trace inequalities across different dimensions, while heatmaps illustrate substantial GPU speedups over CPU for various linear algebra operations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the library structure, validates its implementation against analytical expectations (e.g., Haar moments), details multiple experiments testing quantum observables ($z$), and concludes with performance benchmarks and future work directions.
why_interesting: While mathematically abstract, the focus on GPU-accelerated simulation of structured operators is highly relevant for simulating open quantum systems or complex Hamiltonians where block-diagonalization simplifies the structure but requires massive computational resources.
